title: Neural Critic’s 10 Best Games of All Time
description: From landmark design breakthroughs to modern masterpieces, these are the ten games Neural Critic believes best represent what the medium can achieve.
body:
Any list claiming to name the best games of all time has to admit one thing immediately: there is no objective formula for greatness. Sales, review scores, influence, technical ambition, and personal attachment all measure different things.

For Neural Critic’s first all-time canon, we are prioritizing five ideas: design influence, quality of execution, longevity, replayability, and how clearly a game’s ideas still communicate today. This is not a list of the most important games ever made, nor a ranking of our favorite memories. It is our current editorial answer to a harder question: which games best demonstrate the possibilities of the medium?
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: The most memorable and influencial games ever created

contentBlocks.text:
Portal 2 is the rare sequel that expands almost every part of its predecessor without losing the elegance that made the original work. Its portal mechanics remain immediately understandable, but Valve keeps combining them with momentum, gels, lasers, light bridges, and environmental timing in ways that constantly reframe what the player thinks is possible.

Its writing is just as important to the experience. Comedy, level design, performance, and pacing reinforce one another instead of competing for attention. Even after the solutions are known, Portal 2 remains a masterclass in teaching complicated spatial ideas without drowning the player in explanation.
contentBlocks.caption: Portal 2 turns a tiny set of rules into one of gaming’s most inventive puzzle campaigns.
contentBlocks.heading: Portal 2
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Chell navigating one of Aperture Science’s portal-based test chambers.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A puzzle game that never stops finding new ideas

contentBlocks.text:
Super Metroid helped define an entire vocabulary for exploration games. Doors, terrain, enemy placement, ability gates, and tiny environmental details quietly teach the player how Zebes works. Progress feels earned because new abilities do more than unlock doors—they change how familiar spaces are understood.

What makes the game endure is restraint. It rarely needs lengthy dialogue or explicit navigation markers because its world is built to communicate through shape, sound, and possibility. Modern games continue to borrow that language, but Super Metroid still feels unusually confident in how little it needs to say.
contentBlocks.caption: Super Metroid remains one of the clearest examples of world design teaching the player through exploration.
contentBlocks.heading: Super Metroid
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Samus exploring the interconnected caverns of planet Zebes.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Exploration design that still teaches without speaking

contentBlocks.text:
Red Dead Redemption 2 is deliberately slower than most blockbuster open worlds, and that patience is exactly what gives it weight. Riding into a town, caring for a horse, returning to camp, or noticing a stranger at the side of a road can feel meaningful because the world is allowed to exist at a human pace.

Its simulation is sometimes excessive and its controls can be cumbersome, but few games create such a convincing relationship between character, landscape, and routine. Arthur Morgan’s story works because the enormous world around him is not just scenery; it becomes evidence of a life that is changing faster than he can accept.
contentBlocks.caption: Red Dead Redemption 2 uses detail and pacing to make its world feel inhabited rather than assembled.
contentBlocks.heading: Red Dead Redemption 2
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Arthur Morgan riding through the American frontier.
contentBlocks.subtitle: An open world built around observation and consequence

contentBlocks.text:
Half-Life 2 made physics, environmental storytelling, scripted spectacle, and first-person combat feel like parts of one continuous language. The Gravity Gun is still one of the medium’s great design tools because it is simultaneously a weapon, a puzzle mechanic, and an invitation to experiment with the world.

Its greatest achievement is pacing. City 17, Ravenholm, the coast, and the Citadel all feel distinct, yet the campaign rarely breaks its sense of forward movement. Many games have surpassed individual pieces of Half-Life 2, but very few combine so many ideas with this much clarity.
contentBlocks.caption: Half-Life 2 made physics and environmental interaction central to the rhythm of a shooter campaign.
contentBlocks.heading: Half-Life 2
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Gordon Freeman moving through the occupied streets of City 17.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A first-person campaign with almost no wasted motion

contentBlocks.text:
Minecraft’s greatest strength is not any single adventure, boss, biome, or crafting recipe. It is the way a small collection of readable rules can support building, survival, engineering, exploration, role-playing, multiplayer communities, education, and forms of creativity its original design never explicitly demanded.

Few games have given players this much ownership over what playing means. Its blocky world is instantly understandable, but the possibilities inside it are almost impossible to exhaust. That flexibility has made Minecraft less like a conventional release and more like a permanent piece of gaming culture.
contentBlocks.caption: Minecraft endures because its basic rules can support thousands of different kinds of play.
contentBlocks.heading: Minecraft
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A player-built landscape in Minecraft made from colorful blocks.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A ruleset simple enough to become almost anything

contentBlocks.text:
Baldur’s Gate 3 makes an enormous role-playing game feel reactive at a scale that once seemed unrealistic. Conversations, combat arenas, character relationships, quests, and environmental systems overlap constantly, allowing the player to solve problems through persuasion, violence, stealth, magic, improvisation, or wonderfully bad judgment.

Its real achievement is not that every possibility has a bespoke answer. It is that the game is willing to let systems collide and then support the consequences. That generosity makes repeated playthroughs feel less like revisiting content and more like testing a different version of the same world.
contentBlocks.caption: Baldur’s Gate 3 makes player choice feel systemic rather than decorative.
contentBlocks.heading: Baldur’s Gate 3
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A party of adventurers preparing for a choice-driven encounter in Baldur’s Gate 3.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Choice-heavy role-playing without sanding away the chaos

contentBlocks.text:
Dark Souls changed the language of action RPGs by making uncertainty part of the design. Combat asks for patience, death turns knowledge into progression, and Lordran’s looping geography transforms exploration into a form of mastery. A shortcut is not merely convenient—it changes the player’s mental map of the entire world.

Its influence is obvious, but influence alone would not earn this position. Dark Souls still works because its combat, level design, atmosphere, multiplayer ideas, and storytelling all reinforce the same philosophy: pay attention, accept failure, and learn how the world fits together.
contentBlocks.caption: Dark Souls made knowledge, spatial memory, and persistence inseparable from progression.
contentBlocks.heading: Dark Souls
contentBlocks.imageAlt: The Chosen Undead crossing one of Lordran’s interconnected environments.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A world where challenge, discovery, and geography become one system

contentBlocks.text:
Breath of the Wild reimagined open-world structure around what the player can see, wonder about, and physically reach. Mountains are not decorative barriers, distant landmarks are invitations, and a flexible physics-and-chemistry sandbox turns simple environmental problems into opportunities for experimentation.

The game’s most important innovation is trust. It is willing to give players major abilities early, let them approach objectives in unexpected orders, and accept improvised solutions that would break more rigid adventures. That freedom helped redefine what exploration could feel like in a modern open world.
contentBlocks.caption: Breath of the Wild made curiosity itself the main navigation system.
contentBlocks.heading: The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Link overlooking the open landscape of Hyrule in Breath of the Wild.
contentBlocks.subtitle: An open world that trusts curiosity more than instructions

contentBlocks.text:
Super Mario Galaxy treats gravity as a toy. Tiny planets, shifting perspectives, spherical spaces, launch stars, transformations, and constantly changing objectives let Nintendo reinvent platforming rules from one stage to the next without losing the immediate pleasure of simply moving Mario around.

That variety could have made the game feel scattered. Instead, its controls, music, visual clarity, and tightly edited level design create remarkable cohesion. Few games are this generous with new ideas, and even fewer know exactly when to stop using one and move to the next.
contentBlocks.caption: Super Mario Galaxy combines constant invention with exceptionally readable platforming.
contentBlocks.heading: Super Mario Galaxy
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Mario leaping between small planets in a gravity-bending galaxy.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Movement, level design, and imagination in near-perfect balance

contentBlocks.text:
Elden Ring takes ideas that once depended on tight, hostile corridors and proves they can survive at enormous scale. The Lands Between is open, but it rarely feels like a checklist. Sightlines, ruins, terrain, enemy placement, and architectural silhouettes keep creating questions that exploration can answer—or replace with even stranger questions.

Its achievement is the balance between freedom and authorship. Players can wander, overlevel, summon help, specialize into wildly different builds, or throw themselves at a challenge far earlier than intended, yet the world still retains the danger, surprise, and deliberate encounter design associated with FromSoftware’s best work. For Neural Critic’s first all-time list, no game better combines modern scope with uncompromised identity.
contentBlocks.caption: Elden Ring expands the Souls design philosophy into a world built around curiosity and player choice.
contentBlocks.heading: Elden Ring
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A Tarnished overlooking the Lands Between in Elden Ring.
contentBlocks.subtitle: FromSoftware’s design philosophy expanded without losing its mystery
contentBlocks.platforms: PC, PlayStation 4, PlayStation 5, Xbox One, Xbox Series X|S

quickRead: A puzzle game that never stops finding new ideas
Exploration design that still teaches without speaking
An open world built around observation and consequence
conclusion:
==A canon should never be permanent. New games will challenge these choices, older games will be rediscovered, and the qualities we value in interactive design will continue to change.==

==That is why Neural Critic’s Best Games of All Time is intended to be a living editorial franchise rather than a list carved into stone. The important part is not pretending that ten positions can settle decades of gaming history. It is making the case clearly enough that readers can argue with it—and perhaps discover something worth playing along the way.==
